result.markdown: --- id: index aliases: [] tags: [] author: "John Robin Inston" bibliography: references.bib categories: - "Time Series" - SARIMA - Forecasting - "Atmospheric Science" - Statistics - R - Past code-fold: true code-summary: "Show code" date: 2023-05-30 execute: echo: true freeze: auto message: false warning: false fig-align: center number-sections: true subtitle: "Five year ahead forecasts of carbon dioxide levels above Mauna Loa, Hawaii." title: "Forecasting Atmospheric CO2 with SARIMA Models" title-block-banner: true toc: true --- [ PDF report](report.pdf){.btn .btn-outline-primary .btn-sm} [ GitHub](https://github.com/johnrobininston/atmospheric-co2){.btn .btn-outline-primary .btn-sm} ## Information This page is a rework of a project completed for PSTAT 274 (Time Series Analysis) at the University of California Santa Barbara, taught by Prof. Raya Feldman (Spring 2023). The code behind every figure and table is available in the "Show code" blocks. **Abstract.** We select and fit a Seasonal Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average (SARIMA) model to produce accurate five year ahead forecasts of atmospheric CO$_2$ levels above Mauna Loa, Hawaii. We investigate the properties of the series, the suitability of SARIMA models, and whether the forecasts capture future observations. The analysis uses exploratory analysis, model selection with the adjusted Akaike Information Criterion (AICc), diagnostic checking, residual analysis and spectral analysis. Our first choice model, a SARIMA(0,1,3)(0,1,1)$_{12}$, produced approximately Gaussian white noise residuals and accurate forecasts whose confidence intervals captured the true observed values. ## Introduction Many geophysical time series contain seasonal variation. A key example is atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO$_2$) concentration, which has an annual seasonal cycle - largely due to plant photosynthesis and respiration - superimposed on an increasing trend caused primarily by human CO$_2$ production. We examine monthly measurements of atmospheric CO$_2$ above Mauna Loa, Hawaii over the 32 years from 1959 to 1990 [@brockwell1996; @shumway2011]. The aim is a 5 year ahead forecast from a suitable SARIMA model. The workflow is: - **Exploratory analysis:** decomposition, stationarity transformations, autocorrelations and tests for normality and stationarity. - **Model fitting and selection:** stationarity and invertibility checks, coefficient significance and AICc. - **Residual analysis:** portmanteau tests, white noise tests and spectral analysis. We find that the SARIMA(0,1,3)(0,1,1)$_{12}$ model is the best candidate, and that its residuals, forecasts and spectral decomposition support its use. All analysis was performed in R. ## Data ### Description The data are monthly measurements of atmospheric CO$_2$ above Mauna Loa from January 1959 to December 1990, in parts per million (ppm). They were collected by the Scripps Institution of Oceanography, La Jolla, California and are available through the `tsdl` package [@hyndman2019]. Missing values in the raw data were filled by linear interpolation. The raw series $x_t,~t=1,\dots,384$ has 384 observations. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # libraries library(tsdl) # source for data library(zoo) # rollmean library(ggplot2) # plots and figures library(tidyr) # reshaping data library(gridExtra) # multiple ggplots library(forecast) # seasonal plot, Arima library(tseries) # adf and kpss tests library(knitr) # tables library(astsa) # acf2 library(LSTS) # Ljung-Box plot library(TSA) # periodogram library(ggpubr) # qqplot library(lmtest) # coeftest library(ggplottimeseries) # time series decomposition # remotes::install_github("brisneve/ggplottimeseries") theme_set(theme_minimal()) set.seed(8467) # plot the roots of an AR / MA polynomial against the unit circle plot.roots <- function(ar.roots = NULL, ma.roots = NULL, size = 2, angles = FALSE, special = NULL, sqecial = NULL, my.pch = 1, first.col = "blue", second.col = "red", main = NULL) { xylims <- c(-size, size) omegas <- seq(0, 2 * pi, pi / 500) temp <- exp(complex(real = rep(0, length(omegas)), imag = omegas)) plot(Re(temp), Im(temp), typ = "l", xlab = "x", ylab = "y", xlim = xylims, ylim = xylims, main = main) abline(v = 0, lty = "dotted") abline(h = 0, lty = "dotted") if (!is.null(ar.roots)) { points(Re(1 / ar.roots), Im(1 / ar.roots), col = first.col, pch = my.pch) points(Re(ar.roots), Im(ar.roots), col = second.col, pch = my.pch) } if (!is.null(ma.roots)) { points(Re(1 / ma.roots), Im(1 / ma.roots), pch = "*", cex = 1.5, col = first.col) points(Re(ma.roots), Im(ma.roots), pch = "*", cex = 1.5, col = second.col) } if (angles) { if (!is.null(ar.roots)) { abline(a = 0, b = Im(ar.roots[1]) / Re(ar.roots[1]), lty = "dotted") abline(a = 0, b = Im(ar.roots[2]) / Re(ar.roots[2]), lty = "dotted") } if (!is.null(ma.roots)) { sapply(seq_along(ma.roots), function(j) abline(a = 0, b = Im(ma.roots[j]) / Re(ma.roots[j]), lty = "dotted")) } } if (!is.null(special)) lines(Re(special), Im(special), lwd = 2) if (!is.null(sqecial)) lines(Re(sqecial), Im(sqecial), lwd = 2) } ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # load the monthly CO2 series from the Time Series Data Library tsdl_met <- subset(tsdl, 12, "Meteorology") rawdata <- tsdl_met[[2]] ``` ::: ### Exploratory Analysis We split the data into disjoint training and testing sets. The testing set contains the last 5 years (60 months) of observed CO$_2$ and is used to assess the forecasts of the final model. The training set contains 324 observations. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} data <- head(rawdata, n = length(rawdata) - (12 * 5)) ``` ::: @fig-raw shows the training data with a 12 month moving average. There is a clear increasing polynomial trend and a seasonal component with a 12 month period, so the raw data are non-stationary. The variance appears constant and there are no sharp changes in behaviour, which suggests a SARIMA model should suit the data. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # 12 month moving average maline <- rollmean(data, k = 12, fill = NA, align = "right") plotdata <- data.frame( "Time" = seq(as.Date("1959/1/1"), as.Date("1985/12/1"), "months"), "data" = data, "trend" = maline ) plotdata %>% tidyr::gather("id", "value", 2:3) %>% ggplot(., aes(Time, value, col = id, linetype = id)) + geom_line() + theme_light() + labs(x = "Time", y = "CO2 (ppm)", color = "Legend", linetype = "Legend") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Atmospheric carbon dioxide above Mauna Loa, Hawaii.](index_files/figure-html/fig-raw-1.png){#fig-raw width=960} ::: ::: The decomposition in @fig-decomp separates the seasonal and trend components. There is no evidence of heteroscedastic behaviour in the residuals, so we do not transform the data. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ts_decomp <- ggdecompose(dts2(data, type = "additive")) + xlab("Date") + ylab("Atmospheric Concentration of CO2") + ggtitle("Time Series Decomposition Plots") seasplot <- ggseasonplot(data, year.labels = TRUE, year.labels.left = TRUE) + ylab("CO2 (ppm)") + ggtitle("Seasonal plot") + theme_minimal() trendplot <- autoplot(maline, ts.color = "red", main = "Trend plot") + theme_minimal() grid.arrange(ts_decomp, seasplot, trendplot, layout_matrix = rbind(c(1, 1), c(2, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Time series decomposition, seasonal plot and trend plot.](index_files/figure-html/fig-decomp-1.png){#fig-decomp width=1152} ::: ::: The autocorrelation function (ACF) in @fig-acf-raw shows highly significant autocorrelations for all lags up to 40, which decay slowly and show seasonality. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} acf2(data, 40, main = "ACF and PACF of raw data.") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![ACF and PACF of the raw data.](index_files/figure-html/fig-acf-raw-1.png){#fig-acf-raw width=960} ::: ::: ### Differencing We difference first with lag 12 to remove the seasonal component: $$ y_t = x_t - x_{t-12} = (1-B^{12})x_t = \nabla_{12}x_t, $$ where $B$ is the back-shift operator, $B^kx_t = x_{t-k}$. @fig-diff12 shows that the seasonal pattern is gone but a linear trend remains, and the ACF decays slowly as is typical of data with a polynomial trend. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} data_d <- diff(data, 12) plot_data_d <- data.frame( "Time" = seq(as.Date("1960/1/1"), as.Date("1985/12/1"), "months"), "yt" = data_d ) tsplot_data_d <- plot_data_d %>% tidyr::gather("id", "value", 2:2) %>% ggplot(., aes(Time, value)) + geom_line() + theme_minimal() + labs(x = "Time", y = "Seasonally Differenced Monthly CO2") + geom_smooth(method = lm) acfplot_data_d <- autoplot(acf(data_d, lag = 40, plot = FALSE)) grid.arrange(tsplot_data_d, acfplot_data_d, ncol = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Time series and ACF of the seasonally differenced data.](index_files/figure-html/fig-diff12-1.png){#fig-diff12 width=1152} ::: ::: We difference again with lag 1 to remove the linear trend: $$ u_t = y_t - y_{t-1} = (1-B)y_t = (1-B)(1-B^{12})x_t = \nabla_1\nabla_{12}x_t. $$ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} data_dd <- diff(data_d, 1) plot_data_dd <- data.frame( "Time" = seq(as.Date("1960/2/1"), as.Date("1985/12/1"), "months"), "yt" = data_dd ) plot_data_dd %>% tidyr::gather("id", "value", 2:2) %>% ggplot(., aes(Time, value)) + geom_line() + theme_minimal() + labs(x = "Time", y = "Transformed Data (ut)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Time series plot of the differenced and seasonally differenced data.](index_files/figure-html/fig-diff1-1.png){#fig-diff1 width=960} ::: ::: The twice differenced data appear stationary, with no seasonality or trend and a stable variance. Each transformation lowered the variance of the data (@tbl-var). ::: {#tbl-var .cell tbl-cap='Variance of the data after each transformation.'} ```{.r .cell-code} var_table <- data.frame( "Transformation" = c("None", "Differenced lag 12", "Differenced lag 12 and lag 1"), "Variance" = c(var(data), var(data_d), var(data_dd)) ) kable(var_table) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |Transformation | Variance| |:----------------------------|----------:| |None | 86.0367259| |Differenced lag 12 | 0.3449074| |Differenced lag 12 and lag 1 | 0.1577327| ::: ::: The ACF, histogram and Q-Q plot in @fig-dd-diag show no remaining polynomial or seasonal trend, and an empirical distribution that is symmetric and approximately Gaussian. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} acf_data_dd <- autoplot(acf(data_dd, lag = 40, plot = FALSE)) hist_data_dd <- ggplot(data.frame("data" = data_dd), aes(x = data)) + geom_histogram(color = "darkblue", fill = "lightblue") + ggtitle("Histogram") qqplot_data_dd <- ggqqplot(data_dd, color = "darkblue") + ggtitle("Q-Q plot") grid.arrange(acf_data_dd, hist_data_dd, qqplot_data_dd, ncol = 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![ACF, histogram and Q-Q plot of the twice differenced data.](index_files/figure-html/fig-dd-diag-1.png){#fig-dd-diag width=1248} ::: ::: Finally, we run two stationarity tests. The Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test has a unit root (and hence a trend) as its null, so a large p-value indicates a trend. The Kwiatkowski-Phillips-Schmidt-Shin (KPSS) test has trend stationarity as its null, so a small p-value indicates a unit root. Both conclude that the twice differenced data are trend stationary (@tbl-stat). ::: {#tbl-stat .cell tbl-cap='Trend stationarity test results.'} ```{.r .cell-code} adf_test <- adf.test(data_dd) kpss_test <- kpss.test(data_dd, null = "Trend") table_data <- data.frame( Test = c("ADF Test", "KPSS Test"), Null = c("Process has a unit root and therefore a trend.", "Process is trend stationary"), pValue = c(signif(adf_test$p.value, 2), signif(kpss_test$p.value, 2)), Conclusion = c("Data is trend stationary", "Data is trend stationary") ) kable(table_data) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |Test |Null | pValue|Conclusion | |:---------|:----------------------------------------------|------:|:------------------------| |ADF Test |Process has a unit root and therefore a trend. | 0.01|Data is trend stationary | |KPSS Test |Process is trend stationary | 0.10|Data is trend stationary | ::: ::: ## Model Fitting ### Parameter Selection A SARIMA model has seven parameters: $p, d, q, P, D, Q$ and $s$. Since we differenced once at lag 1 and once at lag 12, we have $d=1$, $D=1$ and $s=12$. To bound the AR parameters $p, P$ and MA parameters $q, Q$ we inspect the ACF and PACF of the differenced data (@fig-acf-dd). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} acf2(data_dd, 60, main = "ACF and PACF of transformed data") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![ACF and PACF of the transformed data.](index_files/figure-html/fig-acf-dd-1.png){#fig-acf-dd width=960} ::: ::: - **Non-seasonal AR ($p$):** the PACF has significant spikes at lags 1 and 3, so we may need up to $p=3$. Spikes at lags 9 and 11 are likely interactions with the seasonal terms. - **Non-seasonal MA ($q$):** the ACF has significant spikes at lags 1 and 3, so we may need up to $q=3$. - **Seasonal AR ($P$):** the PACF is significant at lags 12, 24 and 36, so we may need up to $P=3$. - **Seasonal MA ($Q$):** the ACF is significant at lag 12 only, so we likely need $Q=1$. ### Model Selection We fit, evaluate and compare models using the AICc. Since the AICc penalises large numbers of parameters, we start from the simplest models and add parameters with the aim of minimising the AICc. A full summary of every model considered is given in the [appendix](#summary-of-fitted-models). #### Pure Moving Average Models We first fix $p=P=0$ and find the best pure moving average model, with up to $q=3$ and $Q=1$. The two best models are below. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # SARIMA(0,1,3)(0,1,1)12 model1 <- Arima(data, order = c(0, 1, 3), seasonal = list(order = c(0, 1, 1), period = 12), method = "ML") # SARIMA(0,1,3)(0,1,1)12 with MA2 = 0 model2 <- Arima(data, order = c(0, 1, 3), seasonal = list(order = c(0, 1, 1), period = 12), method = "ML", fix = c(NA, 0, NA, NA)) ``` ::: ::: {#tbl-ma layout-ncol=2} ::: {#tbl-ma-1 .cell tbl-cap='SARIMA(0,1,3)(0,1,1)$_{12}$'} ::: {.cell-output-display} | | Est| SE| z| p| |:----|-------:|------:|--------:|------:| |ma1 | -0.3562| 0.0569| -6.2632| 0.0000| |ma2 | 0.0036| 0.0614| 0.0581| 0.9537| |ma3 | -0.1570| 0.0550| -2.8542| 0.0043| |sma1 | -0.8385| 0.0360| -23.2909| 0.0000| ::: ::: ::: {#tbl-ma-2 .cell tbl-cap='SARIMA(0,1,3)(0,1,1)$_{12}$ with MA2 = 0'} ::: {.cell-output-display} | | Estimate| Std. Error| z value| Pr(>|z|)| |:----|--------:|----------:|--------:|------------------:| |ma1 | -0.3550| 0.0531| -6.6804| 0.0000| |ma3 | -0.1560| 0.0521| -2.9923| 0.0028| |sma1 | -0.8384| 0.0360| -23.2972| 0.0000| ::: ::: Best pure moving average models. AICc: 119.57 (left), 117.51 (right). ::: The MA(2) coefficient of the first model is insignificant, so we fix it to zero and refit. This lowers the AICc from 119.57 to 117.51 and leaves all coefficients significant, making it our top pure MA model. #### Autoregressive Terms We next test whether AR terms reduce the AICc by more than their penalty. The two best candidates are below. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # SARIMA(1,1,1)(0,1,1)12 modelB <- Arima(data, order = c(1, 1, 1), seasonal = list(order = c(0, 1, 1), period = 12), method = "ML") # SARIMA(3,1,1)(0,1,1)12 with AR1 = AR2 = 0 armodel2 <- Arima(data, order = c(3, 1, 1), seasonal = list(order = c(0, 1, 1), period = 12), method = "ML", fixed = c(0, 0, NA, NA, NA)) ``` ::: ::: {#tbl-ar layout-ncol=2} ::: {#tbl-ar-1 .cell tbl-cap='SARIMA(1,1,1)(0,1,1)$_{12}$'} ::: {.cell-output-display} | | Estimate| Std. Error| z value| Pr(>|z|)| |:----|--------:|----------:|--------:|------------------:| |ar1 | 0.3446| 0.1514| 2.2770| 0.0228| |ma1 | -0.6753| 0.1232| -5.4823| 0.0000| |sma1 | -0.8391| 0.0356| -23.5934| 0.0000| ::: ::: ::: {#tbl-ar-2 .cell tbl-cap='SARIMA(3,1,1)(0,1,1)$_{12}$ with AR1 = AR2 = 0'} ::: {.cell-output-display} | | Estimate| Std. Error| z value| Pr(>|z|)| |:----|--------:|----------:|--------:|------------------:| |ar3 | -0.1385| 0.0566| -2.4480| 0.0144| |ma1 | -0.3468| 0.0558| -6.2132| 0.0000| |sma1 | -1.1964| 0.0522| -22.9296| 0.0000| ::: ::: Best models with autoregressive terms. AICc: 123.37 (left), 119.96 (right). ::: Adding seasonal AR terms typically increased the AICc and rarely gave significant coefficients. The SARIMA(1,1,1)(0,1,1)$_{12}$ model performs reasonably well, with all coefficients significant and an AICc of 123.37. The SARIMA(3,1,1)(0,1,1)$_{12}$ model with AR1 = AR2 = 0 has the second best AICc (119.96) but is not viable, since the absolute value of its seasonal MA coefficient is greater than 1. We therefore take the SARIMA(1,1,1)(0,1,1)$_{12}$ model as our second candidate. The two candidates are: **Model (A)** $$ \nabla_1\nabla_{12}X_t=(1-0.354998_{(0.053140)}B-0.155974_{(0.052126)}B^3) (1-0.838438_{(0.035989)}B^{12})Z_t,\quad \hat\sigma_Z^2=0.08431 $$ **Model (B)** $$ \nabla_1\nabla_{12}(1-0.344624_{(0.151353)}B)X_t= (1-0.675336_{(0.123186)}B)(1-0.839105_{(0.035565)}B^{12})Z_t,\quad \hat\sigma_Z^2=0.08583 $$ where $Z_t$ is white noise (WN) with $\mathbb{E}Z_t=0$ and $\operatorname{Var}(Z_t)=\sigma_Z^2$. Model (A) is pure moving average, so it is always stationary. In @fig-roots all MA roots lie outside the unit circle and $|\Theta_1|<1$, so the model is invertible. Model (B) is invertible since $|\theta_1|<1$ and $|\Theta_1|<1$, and stationary since $|\phi_1|<1$. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # final models finalmodel1 <- Arima(data, order = c(0, 1, 3), seasonal = list(order = c(0, 1, 1), period = 12), method = "ML", fix = c(NA, 0, NA, NA)) finalmodel2 <- Arima(data, order = c(1, 1, 1), seasonal = list(order = c(0, 1, 1), period = 12), method = "ML", fixed = c(NA, NA, NA)) plot.roots(NULL, polyroot(c(1, 0.354998, 0, -0.155974)), main = "Roots of the non-seasonal MA part") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Model (A): roots of the non-seasonal MA polynomial.](index_files/figure-html/fig-roots-1.png){#fig-roots width=480} ::: ::: ## Diagnostic Checking For each candidate we plot the residuals alongside their ACF, PACF, histogram, Q-Q plot and Ljung-Box statistics, then run a set of residual tests. The helper below builds both for a fitted model. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # residual diagnostic plots for a fitted model resid_plots <- function(fit) { r <- fit$residuals grid.arrange( autoplot(r, ylab = "Residuals"), autoplot(acf(r, plot = FALSE)) + ggtitle("ACF plot"), ggplot(data.frame("data" = r), aes(x = data)) + geom_histogram(color = "darkblue", fill = "lightblue") + ggtitle("Histogram"), autoplot(pacf(r, plot = FALSE)) + ggtitle("PACF plot"), ggqqplot(r, color = "darkblue") + ggtitle("Q-Q plot"), Box.Ljung.Test(r, lag = 30), layout_matrix = rbind(c(1, 1), c(2, 3), c(4, 5), c(6, 6)) ) } # residual tests for a fitted model resid_tests <- function(fit) { r <- fit$residuals sw <- shapiro.test(r) bp <- Box.test(r, lag = 18, type = "Box-Pierce", fitdf = 3) lb <- Box.test(r, lag = 18, type = "Ljung-Box", fitdf = 3) lbs <- Box.test(r^2, lag = 18, type = "Ljung-Box", fitdf = 0) data.frame( "Test" = c("Shapiro-Wilk", "Box-Pierce", "Ljung-Box", "Ljung-Box (squared)"), "p-value" = c(sw$p.value, bp$p.value, lb$p.value, lbs$p.value), "Conclusion" = c("Normal", "Independence", "No autocorrelation in residuals", "No autocorrelation in squared residuals") ) } ``` ::: ### Model (A) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} resid_plots(finalmodel1) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Model (A): residual analysis plots.](index_files/figure-html/fig-resid-a-1.png){#fig-resid-a width=1152} ::: ::: The residuals show the characteristics of white noise, with no trend, seasonality or conditional heteroscedasticity. The ACF and PACF show no significant spikes up to lag 25, apart from a borderline spike at lag 9. Bar a lower outlier, the histogram and Q-Q plot are consistent with a Gaussian distribution. The Ljung-Box p-values are not significant at any lag up to 30. ::: {#tbl-resid-a .cell tbl-cap='Model (A): residual test results.'} ```{.r .cell-code} kable(resid_tests(finalmodel1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |Test | p.value|Conclusion | |:-------------------|---------:|:---------------------------------------| |Shapiro-Wilk | 0.3162723|Normal | |Box-Pierce | 0.8187969|Independence | |Ljung-Box | 0.7928839|No autocorrelation in residuals | |Ljung-Box (squared) | 0.7703434|No autocorrelation in squared residuals | ::: ::: Model (A) passes all four tests. ### Model (B) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} resid_plots(finalmodel2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Model (B): residual analysis plots.](index_files/figure-html/fig-resid-b-1.png){#fig-resid-b width=1152} ::: ::: The residual behaviour is similar, with borderline spikes at lags 2 and 9 and a slightly heavier tailed distribution than Model (A). No Ljung-Box p-values are significant, but they are much closer to the rejection region than for Model (A). ::: {#tbl-resid-b .cell tbl-cap='Model (B): residual test results.'} ```{.r .cell-code} kable(resid_tests(finalmodel2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |Test | p.value|Conclusion | |:-------------------|---------:|:---------------------------------------| |Shapiro-Wilk | 0.5001295|Normal | |Box-Pierce | 0.3947198|Independence | |Ljung-Box | 0.3639211|No autocorrelation in residuals | |Ljung-Box (squared) | 0.7121532|No autocorrelation in squared residuals | ::: ::: Model (B) also passes all four tests. Both models pass diagnostic checking. Because of the slight edge in the residual analysis of Model (A) and its lower AICc, we select Model (A) as the final model. It is also simpler than our initial speculation from the ACF and PACF, so the AICc procedure kept the model parsimonious. ## Forecasting Our final model is the SARIMA(0,1,3)(0,1,1)$_{12}$ model with the MA2 coefficient fixed at 0: $$ \nabla_1\nabla_{12}X_t=(1-0.354998_{(0.053140)}B-0.155974_{(0.052126)}B^3) (1-0.838438_{(0.035989)}B^{12})Z_t,\quad \hat\sigma_Z^2=0.08431 $$ We produce a 5 year (60 month) ahead forecast with approximate 95% prediction bounds (@fig-forecast). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pred.tr <- predict(finalmodel1, n.ahead = 60) U.tr <- pred.tr$pred + 2 * pred.tr$se # upper prediction bound L.tr <- pred.tr$pred - 2 * pred.tr$se # lower prediction bound fc_time <- seq(time(rawdata)[length(rawdata) - 59], time(rawdata)[length(rawdata)], by = (1 / 12)) plot(data, xlim = c(time(data)[1], time(rawdata)[length(rawdata)]), ylim = c(min(data), max(U.tr)), ylab = "CO2 (ppm)") lines(U.tr, col = "blue", lty = "dashed") lines(L.tr, col = "blue", lty = "dashed") lines(fc_time, pred.tr$pred, col = "red") legend("topleft", legend = c("Forecast", "Confidence Bounds"), col = c("red", "blue"), lty = c(1, 2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![60 month forecast of atmospheric CO2 above Mauna Loa, Hawaii.](index_files/figure-html/fig-forecast-1.png){#fig-forecast width=1152} ::: ::: @fig-forecast-zoom focuses on the period since 1980 and overlays the true observed values from the testing set. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(data, xlim = c(time(data)[length(rawdata) - 130], time(rawdata)[length(rawdata)]), ylim = c(330, max(U.tr)), ylab = "CO2 (ppm)") lines(U.tr, col = "blue", lty = "dashed") lines(L.tr, col = "blue", lty = "dashed") lines(fc_time, pred.tr$pred, col = "red") points(fc_time, rawdata[(length(rawdata) - 59):length(rawdata)], pch = 20) legend("topleft", legend = c("Forecast", "Confidence Bounds", "Observed Values"), col = c("red", "blue", "black"), lty = c(1, 2, NA), pch = c(NA, NA, 20)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Forecast with the observed test data overlaid.](index_files/figure-html/fig-forecast-zoom-1.png){#fig-forecast-zoom width=1152} ::: ::: The forecast was successful. The observed values lie inside the confidence region throughout the five year window. Between 1988 and 1990 the forecast lags below the observed values, which approach the upper bound before returning close to the forecast by the end of 1990. Despite the large (and somewhat impractical) forecasting window, the forecast was accurate. ## Spectral Analysis We first compute periodograms of the undifferenced data and of the residuals of the final model (@fig-periodogram). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) periodogram(data) periodogram(finalmodel1$residuals) par(mfrow = c(1, 1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Periodograms of the data (left) and the final model residuals (right).](index_files/figure-html/fig-periodogram-1.png){#fig-periodogram width=1152} ::: ::: The periodogram of the data has a spike near $0.08\approx 1/12$, matching the 12 month period seen in the seasonal plot. The periodogram of the residuals has no dominant frequency, so no significant seasonality remains. Fisher's test detects hidden periodicities of unspecified frequency in the residuals. Its null hypothesis is Gaussian white noise. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(GeneCycle) fisher.g.test(as.numeric(finalmodel1$residuals)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.8882769 ``` ::: ::: The p-value is above 0.05, so there is insufficient evidence to reject Gaussian white noise. A second test is the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, which we apply through the cumulative periodogram of the residuals (@fig-cpgram). The cumulative periodogram stays inside the confidence band for all frequencies, so the residuals pass this test too. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cpgram(finalmodel1$residuals, main = "") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Cumulative periodogram of the final model residuals.](index_files/figure-html/fig-cpgram-1.png){#fig-cpgram width=576} ::: ::: ## Conclusion We determined and fitted a model that gives accurate forecasts of monthly atmospheric CO$_2$ above Mauna Loa, Hawaii (January 1959 to December 1990). Exploratory analysis revealed a linear trend and a 12 month seasonal pattern, both removed by differencing. We fitted a range of SARIMA models and chose the best by AICc and then by residual analysis. The final model is the SARIMA(0,1,3)(0,1,1)$_{12}$ model with MA2 fixed at 0. Its 60 month forecast contained all future observations within the confidence region. Spectral analysis supports the choice, with residuals that are consistent with Gaussian white noise and no remaining seasonality. ## Appendix ### Summary of Fitted Models {#summary-of-fitted-models} Standard errors are omitted.
